title: Cyclic groups and the integers
summary: The division algorithm, gcd and Bézout's identity as the engine of the unit; the subgroup generated by an element and the order of an element; every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic; the order formula n/gcd(k, n) and the generators of Z_n; complex numbers in polar form, De Moivre, the circle group and the cyclic group of nth roots of unity.

objectives.description: State and prove Bézout's identity from the division algorithm and use it to prove Euclid's lemma and the units criterion.
Prove that ⟨a⟩ is the smallest subgroup containing a, that |⟨a⟩| equals the order of a, and that every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic.
Prove the order formula |a^k| = n/gcd(k, n) in a cyclic group of order n and count generators and elements of each order.
Prove that the nth roots of unity form a cyclic group of order n generated by cis(2π/n), identify the primitive roots, and decide whether a given U(n) is cyclic.

preparation.description: Revise Section 2.2: the division algorithm (Theorem 2.2.1), gcd and Bézout (Theorem 2.2.2, Corollary 2.2.3), the Euclidean algorithm (Example 2.2.4), Euclid's lemma (Lemma 2.2.5). Skim the rest of the section.
Read Section 4.1: cyclic subgroups and Theorem 4.1.3, Examples 4.1.5–4.1.7, Theorems 4.1.9–4.1.10 with proofs, Corollary 4.1.11, Proposition 4.1.12, Theorem 4.1.13 with proof, Corollary 4.1.14.

Read Section 4.2: polar form and Proposition 4.2.5, De Moivre (Theorem 4.2.7), the circle group (Proposition 4.2.9), the roots of unity (Theorem 4.2.10) and Example 4.2.11. Section 4.3 (repeated squares) is optional.

activities.title: Sections 2.2, 4.1–4.2: cyclic groups and roots of unity
activities.instructions: Read the lesson alongside Judson. After Theorem 4.1.10, close the text and reprove that every subgroup of Z is of the form nZ using the division algorithm, then compare with the text's proof. Optional: MIT student notes lecture 2 covers the same ground from the viewpoint of subgroups of Z.

activities.title: Tutorial: orders, generators and roots of unity
activities.instructions: Attempt exercise 1, then exercise 2. In exercise 1 prove the general statements before filling in the table for Z_36; in exercise 2 write Bézout's identity explicitly before raising anything to a power. Submit each attempt when you believe it is complete.

activities.title: Explain: why U(8) is not cyclic
activities.instructions: Write exercise 3 without the text open; then check your claims about U(5) and U(10) by computing the powers of your proposed generators.

activities.title: Retrieval: statements of the unit
activities.instructions: From memory, with hypotheses: Bézout's identity; every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic; the order of a^k; the generators of Z_n; the nth roots of unity form a cyclic group of order n.

exitCheck.description: Exercise 1 accepted: one subgroup of each order dividing n, φ(d) elements of order d, the identity Σ_{d|n} φ(d) = n deduced, and the table for Z_36 correct.

commonMisconceptions.claim: U(n) is cyclic for every n.
commonMisconceptions.correction: U(8) = {1, 3, 5, 7} has every element of order at most 2, so no element generates it; a cyclic group of order 4 has an element of order 4. (U(9) is cyclic, Example 4.1.6; which U(n) are cyclic is a theorem of number theory not proved in this course.)

commonMisconceptions.claim: In a cyclic group of order n generated by a, the element a^k has order n/k.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The order is n/gcd(k, n) (Theorem 4.1.13). In Z_6 the element 4 = 4·1 has order 3 = 6/gcd(4, 6), not 6/4.

commonMisconceptions.claim: If every proper subgroup of G is cyclic then G is cyclic.
commonMisconceptions.correction: S_3 has every proper subgroup cyclic (orders 1, 2, 3) but no element of order 6 (Example 4.1.7).

commonMisconceptions.claim: An infinite cyclic group has infinitely many generators.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Z is generated only by 1 and −1: if d generates Z then 1 = dk for some integer k, forcing d = ±1. Compare Z_n, which has φ(n) generators (Corollary 4.1.14).

checks.name: mathematical-review
checks.evidence: Build agent re-derived: Bézout via the least positive element of {ar + ns}; Euclid's lemma; |⟨a⟩| = order of a; subgroups of cyclic groups are cyclic with k | n; the order formula via coprimality of k' and n'; the direct proof that μ_n = ⟨cis(2π/n)⟩ has exactly n elements without the polynomial-roots corollary the text cites; one subgroup per divisor; φ(d) elements of order d and Σ_{d|n} φ(d) = n; the Z_36 table (12, 6, 4, 6, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1 for orders 36, 18, 12, 9, 6, 4, 3, 2, 1); a^{gcd(m,n)} = e; μ_12 ∩ μ_8 = μ_4; primitive 12th roots ω^k for k ∈ {1, 5, 7, 11}; U(5) = ⟨2⟩ and U(10) = ⟨3⟩.

checks.name: answer-leakage
checks.evidence: Reference reasoning lives only in instructor/. The lesson proves the theorems the exercises build on (as the text does) but does not state the Z_36 counts, the intersection formula for roots of unity, or the U(5), U(10) generators; the U(8) warning in the lesson is deliberately the subject of the explain-back, as in the exemplar.
